group.label: MCP Database Reader
group.comment:
Settings for the optional db.query tool — read-only SQL against this store's database. This is the highest-risk tool in the MCP family. It is off by default, gated by its own ACL resource (Tool: Run Read-Only SQL Query), and rejects anything that is not a single SELECT.

Access is allowlist-only: the tool can read the tables named in Allowed Tables and nothing else, and it refuses every query — including SELECT 1 — while that field is empty. A small set of tables (admin accounts, tokens, sessions, core_config_data, the server's own schemas) is protected in code and stays unreadable even if it is listed there.

Even so, a read-only query can still expose customer PII and order history from the tables you do allow. Treat "who may enable this", "which tables are listed" and "which token holds the ACL" as security decisions, not convenience ones.

field.label: Enable Read-Only SQL Tool
field.comment: Default: No. Setting this to Yes lets any MCP token whose admin role holds the Tool: Run Read-Only SQL Query ACL resource read the tables you list in Allowed Tables — nothing more, and nothing at all until that list is filled in. Queries are restricted to a single read-only SELECT. Only enable this if you intend to give those token holders direct read access to the tables you allow, and keep the ACL resource off every role that does not need it.

field.label: Default Row Limit
field.comment: Row cap applied when a query does not ask for one. Keeping this small limits how much data a single careless or hostile call can extract, and how much of it lands in the MCP audit log. Default 100.

field.label: Maximum Row Limit
field.comment: Hard ceiling a caller can never exceed, however large a limit it requests. This is the bulk-exfiltration brake — raising it directly raises how many rows one call can pull out of the store. Default 1000.

field.label: Statement Timeout (seconds)
field.comment: Server-side time budget per query. This is the denial-of-service brake: without it a single unindexed join can pin a database thread and starve the storefront. Raise it only if you accept that risk. Default 10.

field.label: Allowed Tables
field.comment:
The tool can read these tables and no others. One bare table name per line — no schema prefix, no quoting, no wildcards. Blank lines and lines starting with # are ignored. If your install uses a table prefix, list names without it.

Empty means every query is refused, including SELECT 1. That is the shipped default: enabling the tool and deciding what it may see are two separate decisions.

A starting point to paste and trim — not a recommendation to expose these tables. Review every line against your own data-protection obligations, and remove anything you do not actively need:

catalog_product_entity
catalog_product_entity_varchar
catalog_product_entity_int
catalog_product_entity_decimal
catalog_category_entity
catalog_category_product
cataloginventory_stock_item
eav_attribute
eav_entity_type
store
store_website
store_group
cms_page
cms_block
sales_order
sales_order_item
sales_order_status_history

Note that order tables carry customer names, e-mail addresses and totals, and that a few tables (admin accounts, tokens, sessions, core_config_data, the server's own schemas) stay unreadable however they are listed.

field.label: Additional Denied Tables
field.comment:
One table name per line, protected on top of the allowlist. Blank lines and lines starting with # are ignored.

Rarely needed now that access is allowlist-only — its use is belt and braces for a name you want blocked even if someone later adds it to Allowed Tables, and it matches wrapper tables too (a denied my_vault also blocks my_vault_archive). Entries here only ever remove access; they can never grant it.
